name: Vertigo and balance problems (including BPPV and Meniere's disease)
definition: Vertigo is the feeling that you, or the world around you, is moving or spinning, and it is often caused by a problem in the inner ear.
overview: The NHS describes vertigo as a symptom rather than a condition in itself. Inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes, and the NHS lists benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease among them. BPPV causes brief, intense spells of vertigo triggered by a change in head position, while Ménière's disease involves episodes of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in the ear. Most people with vertigo improve without treatment, and treatment depends on the cause.
causes: Inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes of vertigo.
Common causes listed by the NHS are BPPV, labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease.
In BPPV, loose otoconia tumble into one of the semicircular canals and affect how the cupula works.
The cause of Ménière's disease is still unknown according to the NIDCD.
signs: Involuntary eye movements called nystagmus, with vertigo, when the Dix-Hallpike head-position test is carried out in BPPV
complications: BPPV often recurs even though the outlook with appropriate treatment is good
Fluctuating hearing loss in Ménière's disease
diagnosis: BPPV is diagnosed mainly from the history of symptoms and from typical findings on the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre, a head-position test. For Ménière's disease, a medical review says there are no specific diagnostic tests, so diagnosis is clinical and generally needs more than one attack. For suspected Ménière's disease, the NHS says a GP will check the ears, head and neck.
treatment: Treatment depends on the cause; for vertigo in general the NHS says antihistamines can sometimes help and balance exercises may be recommended. BPPV often settles by itself or with canalith repositioning manoeuvres done in a clinic. Ménière's disease cannot be cured, but treatment can help the symptoms, and the NIDCD says diet changes, stopping smoking and anti-vertigo or anti-nausea medicines may be recommended. Surgery is considered for Ménière's disease only when medical treatment has not worked.
prevention: The NHS suggests lifestyle changes such as drinking plenty of fluids, avoiding caffeine, not smoking and not drinking alcohol can help manage Ménière's disease, but the sources reviewed do not describe a way to prevent BPPV.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for double or lost vision, hearing loss, difficulty speaking, or weakness, numbness or tingling in the limbs with vertigo. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised by the NHS when vertigo comes with a severe headache, sickness or a high temperature. A routine GP appointment is advised if vertigo will not go away or keeps coming back.

sections.heading: What is vertigo, and what causes it?
sections.body:
Vertigo is the feeling that you, or the environment around you, is moving or spinning. The NHS describes it as a symptom rather than a condition in itself. Attacks can be short, and sometimes they last much longer. Inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes. The NHS lists benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease as common causes.

BPPV is the most common of these, according to the NHS. Most people with vertigo improve without treatment, and what is done depends on the cause. This page looks mainly at BPPV and Ménière's disease, two inner ear conditions that the NHS and the US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) describe.

sections.heading: What is BPPV and how does it feel?
sections.body:
The NIDCD describes BPPV as a brief, intense episode of vertigo triggered by a specific change in the position of the head. The NHS likewise says specific head movements can bring on the vertigo. A medical review says symptoms are most obvious with changes in position and are usually worse in the morning. It adds that recurrent episodes lasting under a minute are usually BPPV.

An NIDCD handout explains that the condition arises when loose otoconia tumble into one of the semicircular canals and affect how the cupula works. Otoconia are tiny crystals in the inner ear, and the semicircular canals are the fluid-filled loops that sense head movement. The review says BPPV is usually resolved spontaneously or with canalith repositioning manoeuvres carried out in a clinic. The outlook is good with appropriate treatment, but the problem often recurs. Recurrence, or other inner ear symptoms such as hearing loss or tinnitus, can suggest that something else in the ear is involved.

sections.heading: What is Ménière's disease?
sections.body:
The NIDCD describes Ménière's disease as episodes of vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus (a ringing or buzzing in the ear) and a feeling of fullness in the ear. The NHS lists feeling that you or everything around you is spinning, losing your balance and hearing loss among the symptoms. A medical review links recurrent episodes lasting minutes to hours with Ménière's disease, particularly when roaring tinnitus and hearing loss are present.

An NHS Lanarkshire page says attacks usually last a few hours and can go away for long periods. It adds that the symptoms can be very troublesome. The NIDCD says the cause or causes are still unknown. A review describes the mechanism as a disturbance of fluid volume in the inner ear, although the trigger is unclear. The NHS says Ménière's disease cannot be cured, but treatment can help with the symptoms.

sections.heading: How is vertigo diagnosed?
sections.body:
For BPPV, diagnosis rests mainly on the history of symptoms and on typical findings during the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre. NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries (CKS) describes the manoeuvre as a head-position test used when positional vertigo is affected by moving the head. Posterior canal BPPV is diagnosed if the manoeuvre provokes vertigo and torsional, upbeating nystagmus, which means involuntary eye movements. NICE guideline NG127 recommends offering the Hallpike manoeuvre to adults with transient rotational vertigo on head movement, and offering canalith repositioning if BPPV is diagnosed.

For Ménière's disease, a review says there are no specific diagnostic tests, so the diagnosis is a clinical one that generally needs more than one attack. It says the diagnosis should come from a specialist with a focus on vestibular disorders. The NHS says a GP will check the ears, head and neck when Ménière's disease is suspected. NG127 also asks clinicians to be alert to vestibular migraine, which is migraine-associated vertigo, in adults with episodes lasting from 5 minutes to 72 hours. It lists sudden-onset dizziness with a focal neurological deficit as a pattern needing particular attention.

sections.heading: How are BPPV and Ménière's disease treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment for vertigo depends on the cause. It adds that antihistamines can sometimes help and that balance exercises may be recommended. For BPPV, NHS audiology leaflets describe the Epley manoeuvre, a set of four head movements, as something a doctor may try. NICE guideline NG127 recommends offering canalith repositioning when BPPV is diagnosed.

For Ménière's disease, the NHS says care aims to ease symptoms and that tinnitus may also need treatment. The NIDCD says a specialist ear, nose and throat doctor (otolaryngologist) may recommend changes to diet and, for smokers, stopping smoking. It adds that anti-vertigo or anti-nausea medicines may help symptoms, though they can cause drowsiness. A review says medical treatment comes before more invasive surgery, which is considered for those who do not respond to medication.

sections.heading: Self-care, living with vertigo and when to get help
sections.body:
For vertigo attacks, the NHS suggests lying still in a dark room, sitting down as soon as dizziness begins, and getting up slowly after lying down. It also suggests a walking stick for people at risk of falling. For Ménière's disease, the NHS says drinking lots of fluids, avoiding caffeine, not smoking and not drinking alcohol can help manage it.

A routine GP appointment is advised by the NHS if vertigo does not go away or keeps coming back. An urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 is advised if vertigo comes with a severe headache, sickness or a high temperature. Call 999 or go to A&E if vertigo comes with double or lost vision, hearing loss, difficulty speaking, or weakness, numbness or tingling in the limbs.

faqs.q: Is vertigo the same as dizziness?
faqs.a: Vertigo is the feeling that you or your surroundings are moving or spinning. The NHS describes it as a symptom rather than a condition in itself. Inner ear problems are the most common causes, and the NHS lists BPPV, labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease. Treatment depends on the cause, and most people improve without treatment.

faqs.q: Does BPPV go away on its own?
faqs.a: A medical review says BPPV is usually resolved spontaneously or with canalith repositioning manoeuvres done in a clinic. The same review says the outlook is good with appropriate treatment, but that BPPV often recurs. A GP can advise on whether the pattern fits BPPV, and a routine appointment is the usual route if vertigo keeps returning.

The NHS says Ménière's disease cannot be cured, but treatment can help with the symptoms. The NIDCD says the cause is still unknown. Treatment may include diet changes, stopping smoking and medicines for vertigo or nausea, according to the NIDCD. A review says surgery is considered only when medical treatment has not worked.

faqs.q: What is the difference between BPPV and Ménière's disease?
faqs.a: The NIDCD describes BPPV as a brief, intense episode of vertigo triggered by a specific change in head position. It describes Ménière's disease as episodes of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in the ear. A review says recurrent episodes under a minute are usually BPPV, while episodes lasting minutes to hours with roaring tinnitus and hearing loss point towards Ménière's disease.

faqs.q: When should vertigo be treated as an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if vertigo comes with double or lost vision, hearing loss, difficulty speaking, or limb weakness, numbness or tingling. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for vertigo with a severe headache, sickness or a high temperature.
